main_damage_causes: Absence of the deathday party (Book 2) strips Nick of his most extended characterization — his vanity, loneliness, friendship with Harry, and humiliation by the Headless Hunt — reducing him to a functional cameo character.

Absence of the post-Sirius death conversation (Book 5) removes Nick's only moment of genuine dramatic depth and tragic self-awareness, which also weakens Harry's grief arc and the saga's thematic engagement with death and choice.

Nick's voice and personality are consistently flattened in his film appearances — the stiff wounded dignity, emotional bitterness about the Headless Hunt, and layered self-consciousness that make him distinctive in the books are replaced with brief comic gags.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Nearly Headless Nick's introduction at the feast
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Nick as the Gryffindor ghost who initiates conversation with the first years, watches food with sad longing, introduces himself as 'Sir Nicholas de Mimsy-Porpington,' is stiff about his preferred name, and demonstrates his near-decapitation with irritable pride — showing a character who is both dignified and comedically self-conscious about his status.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nick pops out of a bowl and immediately says 'Hello! How are you? Welcome to Gryffindor' before Ron identifies him as Nearly Headless Nick. Nick says 'I prefer Sir Nicholas if you don't mind' — a single corrective line with no context of bitterness or dignity. He then demonstrates his head without the irritable reluctance the book gives him. His mournful watching of food is reduced to a brief visual beat with no dialogue establishing his longing or his 400-year deprivation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Nick is proudly stiff about his name and reveals the near-decapitation with irritated showmanship after being goaded. The film collapses this into a quick gag, losing the layered combination of wounded dignity, social pretension, and self-deprecating humor that defines his voice. His longing for food — a key humanizing detail — is also stripped of its verbal pathos.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Nick's mention of the Headless Hunt rejection
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The Headless Hunt rejection is a running source of genuine bitterness for Nick — in Book 2 he is found muttering morosely about it, erupts with barely suppressed fury reading Sir Patrick's letter, and the humiliation shapes his emotional state through the deathday party sequence. It is a meaningful character wound.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nick mentions at the feast, in a single throwaway line, 'Once again, my request to join the headless hunt has been denied.' It is played as a brief comedic aside with no visible bitterness or weight.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Headless Hunt rejection is one of Nick's defining ongoing humiliations. Reducing it to a single flat line with no emotional texture removes the sense that this genuinely wounds his pride and strips the deathday party (which does not appear in the film corpus) of its motivational context.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 (Chamber of Secrets) — Nearly Headless Nick petrified alongside Justin
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Nick as 'pearly-white and transparent' floating immobile and horizontal, with his face wearing 'an expression of shock identical to Justin's.' The discovery triggers widespread school panic specifically because people realize a ghost — someone already dead — has been harmed, which is uniquely terrifying. Nick's petrification has narrative and thematic weight as evidence of the basilisk's extraordinary power.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nick is shown inert and 'body teeming with black smoke' on the floor. The film preserves the discovery beat but significantly compresses the communal panic and the specific horror of a ghost being petrified. Nick is essentially a prop in this scene — he has no dialogue and his condition is used purely to move Harry toward Dumbledore's office.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Nick's petrification is faithfully depicted in broad strokes, so damage is limited. However, the film does not convey the specific communal terror that the books describe — that Nick's fate 'seemed to worry people most' because it raised the question of what could harm someone already dead. This thematic resonance is absent.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 — Harry deduces basilisk method via Nearly Headless Nick in the corridor scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the books, Harry works out that Justin saw the basilisk through Nick — 'Justin must've seen the basilisk through Nearly Headless Nick! Nick got the full blast of it, but he couldn't die again.' This is part of Harry's key deductive moment. Nick's petrification is thus essential to solving the mystery.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 12 (the corridor scene where Harry reads Hermione's torn page), Harry says the same deduction: 'Justin must've seen the Basilisk through Nearly Headless Nick! Nick got the full blast of it, but he's a ghost — he couldn't die again.' This is faithfully preserved.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a faithful moment — no damage. Nick's plot function as the indirect basilisk shield for Justin is correctly retained.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 (Chamber of Secrets) — Absence of the deathday party
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus contains extensive deathday party material: Nick personally invites Harry, the party is organized by Nick as a social event of great personal importance to him (his 500th deathday), it shows his loneliness and vanity, his resentment of Sir Patrick's arrival, his failed speech, and his attempt to maintain dignity while being publicly humiliated. Harry defending him to Sir Patrick shows their friendship. The entire sequence is a defining characterization block for Nick.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The deathday party does not appear in the film corpus at all. Nick's 500th deathday, his invitation to Harry, his hosting of the event, his humiliation by the Headless Hunt, and the relationship dynamic with Harry are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The deathday party is the single largest block of Nearly Headless Nick characterization in the books. Its absence removes: his social vanity and need for recognition, the depth of his friendship with Harry (who attends out of loyalty), his genuine vulnerability and humiliation, the comedic rivalry with Sir Patrick, and the ghost-community world-building. This is the most significant omission for Nick's character overall, reducing him from a fleshed-out recurring character to a functional cameo.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 — Nick's role in helping Gryffindors navigate the castle (Book 1 context)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes that Nick was 'always happy to point new Gryffindors in the right direction' and serves as a helpful, familiar presence in the castle corridors — a mentor-adjacent figure for new students.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This role is entirely absent from the film. Nick's only appearance in the first film is the feast introduction. His corridor-guidance function and friendly relationship with students beyond brief comic appearances is not depicted.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor omission — this establishes Nick as genuinely integrated into Hogwarts life rather than just a gag character, but its absence is partly compensated by Percy's role as guide in the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film (Order of the Phoenix corpus) — Absence of Nick's conversation with Harry about Sirius and death
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book 5 contains one of Nick's most important scenes: Harry seeks him out after Sirius's death, and Nick delivers a profound, emotionally resonant conversation about his own choice to become a ghost out of fear of death, explaining that Sirius 'will have gone on' and cannot return as a ghost, and admitting 'I was afraid of death... I chose to remain behind. I sometimes wonder whether I oughtn't to have.' This is Nick's most emotionally significant moment in the entire series — it reframes his comic existence as a tragedy and deepens the saga's themes about death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear anywhere in the Order of the Phoenix film corpus provided. The film corpus for OotP contains no Nick scenes at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence for Nick's character across the saga. The conversation with Harry after Sirius's death is Nick's defining dramatic moment — it transforms him from comic relief into a genuinely tragic figure who chose a 'feeble imitation of life' out of cowardice, and it provides Harry (and the audience) with crucial thematic closure about death, choice, and moving on. Its absence also weakens Harry's grief arc at a pivotal moment. Nick's entire characterization suffers because his one scene of genuine depth and narrative weight is never shown.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Sorcerer's Stone) — Nick comments on Harry becoming Seeker
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: No specific book baseline for this exact exchange — the book does not have Nick comment on Harry's Seeker appointment in this way.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Nick says 'Have you heard? Harry Potter's the new Gryffindor Seeker. I always knew he'd do well.' This is a brief, positive characterization consistent with his book role as a Gryffindor booster.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a minor film addition that is broadly consistent with Nick's book characterization as a Gryffindor-proud figure. Negligible damage — if anything slightly positive, though the line lacks the book's more nuanced voice.
